title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Lecture, Q&A with students of Peking Univ. (Guanghua School of Mgmt.)–Dec. 3, 2020
summary: Pabrai presents his brand-new 'spawners' framework, born of a 2020 investing 'renaissance': companies whose DNA is to keep incubating new businesses (adjacent, embryonic, cloner, non-adjacent, and rare 'apex' spawners like Amazon, Alphabet, Alibaba, Tencent). He argues growing pies beat discounted pies, lays out market-cap rules for 10x/100x returns, warns against fake spawners like CMGI, and in Q&A covers management DNA, bet sizing, Nick Sleep's Nomad, Costco, Seritage, circle of competence, and leverage as his biggest source of mistakes.

ideas.idea: Investors face two options, growing pies and discounted pies, and growing pies are the better path because they allow set-it-and-forget-it and 10x-100x outcomes.
ideas.detail: Discounted 40-50 cent dollars put you on a tax-inefficient treadmill of buying and selling and rarely deliver more than a double or triple; growing pies with long runways can be held indefinitely even at optically expensive prices.

ideas.idea: He switched from growing pies to discounted pies around 2000 because of the bubble, but should have switched back three to five years ago.
ideas.detail: He captured a 200-bagger in the 1994-99 boom, then saw froth by late 1999; the day NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low near $40,000. NASDAQ was flat from 2000 to 2016 and the S&P flat till about 2012, so discounted pies worked, but he stayed too long.

ideas.idea: There are five paths to 10-100 baggers: focused mouse traps, great capital allocators, uber cannibals, deeply undervalued players, and spawners.
ideas.detail: Examples: Moutai and McDonald's as focused players; Berkshire, Danaher and Exor as allocators; NVR bought back 82% of shares since 1996 for a 70x+ return with little business growth; Teledyne under Henry Singleton bought back 80%+ of stock for 125x from 1960-1980; Teck Cominco was a 10-bagger from 2009 and Fiat Chrysler from 2012.

ideas.idea: Spawners, companies whose DNA is to continuously incubate related and unrelated businesses, are the focus of his 2020 investing renaissance.
ideas.detail: Very few companies have spawning DNA; they expect many bets to fail and take failure in stride, as in Bezos's 'experiment patiently, accept failures, plant seeds, protect saplings, double down when you see customer delight'.

ideas.idea: Spawning is more capital-efficient than cannibalizing because reinvesting cash flows reduces reported income and taxes, an interest-free loan from the government.
ideas.detail: Cannibals must pay tax on earnings before buying back shares; Amazon reported almost no earnings for most of its history while its profitable core funded new bets, and 30-40% of that money would otherwise have gone to the government.

ideas.idea: Spawners come in types: adjacent, embryonic (buy and nurture), cloner (copy successful products), non-adjacent, and rare apex spawners that do all four.
ideas.detail: Amazon adding categories beyond books is adjacent; Microsoft buying Forethought (PowerPoint) is embryonic; Microsoft cloning Windows, Word, Excel, Explorer, Azure, Teams is cloner; BYD entering N95 masks is non-adjacent. Apex spawners like Amazon, Alphabet, Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu and Berkshire have many roads to Nirvana, like a Swiss Army knife.

ideas.idea: Kotak Mahindra was a spawner he bought in 1995 and dumbly sold in 2000 with almost no return; $3,000 held would be about $600,000 today.
ideas.detail: He put $25,000 into Indian stocks in 1995; one became 140x ($10,000 to $1.4 million) in the dotcom boom, and he sold the other three including Kotak for no good reason. Kotak's 2003 banking license and adjacent spawns drove it to one of India's largest private banks.

ideas.idea: Most businesses lack spawning DNA and some, like McDonald's and Ford, deliberately divested good adjacent businesses as distractions.
ideas.detail: McDonald's took a 20-30% stake in Chipotle at 20-30 stores and sold it as a distraction; Alan Mulally sold Land Rover and Jaguar in 2009 to focus on the Ford brand. Costco and Moutai are also classic focused non-spawners, whereas Walmart has spawned many formats.

ideas.idea: Pabrai's spawning rules: assume no business exceeds $50 billion market cap, so buy below $5 billion for a 10x and below $500 million for a 100x.
ideas.detail: Of 3,700 US IPOs in the last 20 years, only nine now exceed $100 billion. Most 100x returns are captured while a company is private; Alibaba at $800 billion cannot plausibly reach $80 trillion, and Uber, public at $50 billion, is unlikely to be a 100x.

ideas.idea: Spawning cannot be screened for quantitatively; you have to study the business, but a few hours of history usually make the DNA obvious.
ideas.detail: He holds three spawners below $1 billion market cap and recently found a fourth below $400 million with a long history; his holy grail is a portfolio of only apex spawners, five to ten names, and finding one a year is enough.

ideas.idea: Every sale is a confession of error; the goal is to be a silent minority partner with a great entrepreneur and ride as long as they ride.
ideas.detail: He cites Thomas Phelps and Nick Sleep's line that 'truly brilliant investors weren't investors, they were entrepreneurs that didn't sell', invoking Jack Ma, Sam Walton and Jeff Bezos.

ideas.idea: Nick Sleep's Nomad shut down in 2014 with 90%+ in Amazon, Costco and Berkshire and told investors to just hold those three without paying fees.
ideas.detail: Nomad managed about $3 billion in 2013 with maybe 60-70% in Amazon near $300 a share; Sleep first bought Amazon at $30 in 2002 and kept buying at $100, $200, $300. One great spawner made up for everything else in a dozen-stock portfolio.

ideas.idea: A portfolio of 5-10 spawners at 10% each can tolerate several duds because two or three home runs pay for all the mistakes.
ideas.detail: His hypothesis is that with careful selection three or four may not work and that is fine; the approach tolerates being wrong, and duds are relatively easy to avoid by checking the track record.

ideas.idea: The first rule of compounding is never to interrupt it; only exit when it is absolutely clear a secular decline has started, even if you give up 50% from the peak.
ideas.detail: Businesses do not go up in a straight line, so ignore temporary headwinds; after a long run, being a little late getting off the bus does not hurt returns, but getting off for a temporary hiccup does.

ideas.idea: Beware fake spawners: CMGI, Satyam and the 1999-2000 internet incubators, and the 2020 SPAC wave looks similar.
ideas.detail: He bought CMGI in 1995 for little more than cash, made 100-140x ($100,000 to $10 million) and got off near the peak because valuation was ridiculous, not because he could tell the spawns were failing. When everyone has a SPAC, it is likely a bubble; set a high bar that spawning must be obviously real.

ideas.idea: The spawner framework changes valuation: instead of valuing 'other bets' at zero, he now pays something extra for the spawning DNA.
ideas.detail: Previously he treated Alphabet's other bets as free upside worth zero; now he would value the core pieces and add maybe $5-10 billion for the DNA, since zero is too extreme, and would have wanted Google at under $5 billion or $500 billion market cap.

ideas.idea: A great spawner never bets the farm; bets are small relative to the mothership, scaled up only as traction appears, and killed quickly when they fail.
ideas.detail: BYD's N95 mask entry would be a rounding error if it failed; Amazon buried the Fire Phone when it got no traction. Elon Musk's indifference to money bothers him because he could make a huge unproven bet, which Bezos would not do.

ideas.idea: Spawners must be founder-led or have a leader with 10-15 years of studyable history; spawning that happened under a founder and then passed to professional management is a red flag.
ideas.detail: All his spawner holdings are founder-led with 10-30 years of history (the Japanese one founded in 1985, public around 2003, founder now 55). Reliance Industries is a case where the second generation is better than the founder, but that takes time to see.

ideas.idea: Missing a spawner like Alibaba or Google is fine; the real error is calling something a spawner when it is not, so it must be obvious.
ideas.detail: Like baseball, there are no called strikes for passing; spawning is a continuum from extreme non-spawner to extreme spawner, and you want only strong spawning DNA. Li Lu's early BYD bet was not a spawner call, but once BYD entered cars it became a keeper.

ideas.idea: To avoid the man-with-a-hammer problem, bounce investment ideas off a candid peer, not an employee, as Munger advised.
ideas.detail: Munger told him he did not always have Warren to talk to but always discussed ideas with a peer; hierarchy blocks candid sharing, and you are the easiest person to fool.

ideas.idea: Stocks drop 20% after he buys them and that never bothers him, because auction-driven markets swing wildly and you are buying a business, not a stock.
ideas.detail: Any Shanghai stock's 52-week range is like 70-150 while home prices move 5-15% a year; if you understand what the business is worth you should be happy to buy more when it drops. 'If wealth is lost, nothing is lost; if character is lost, everything is lost.'

ideas.idea: Investors buy stocks for one reason but sell for a hundred, so nothing can be inferred from Berkshire selling Costco.
ideas.detail: The Costco sale surprised him since Munger loves Costco and talks about it at every dinner; Buffett's actions show he deeply loves Bank of America and less so Wells Fargo now.

ideas.idea: He bought Seritage in Q2 2020 after it fell 70-80% in weeks; it is an 'unspawner' selling assets to stay afloat, bought before the framework, but he is happy with it.
ideas.detail: His two reported US holdings are Micron, held for a couple of years, and Seritage; the steep drop is the clue to his interest.

ideas.idea: The size of your circle of competence is irrelevant; what matters is staying inside it, and running a business first is a huge advantage for investors.
ideas.detail: He could not have built the spawner framework without having done adjacent spawning at his own IT company. Munger's friend John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford; Sam Walton, Ray Kroc and Jim Sinegal had very narrow expertise.

ideas.idea: His biggest source of investing mistakes over 26 years has been companies with too much debt or inherent leverage; a good business should not need debt.
ideas.detail: Many failed investments were leveraged companies or financial services firms; he still holds some leveraged names, 'like an alcoholic who has not given up alcohol yet', but wants to minimize it.
